newsitem.title: JAPAN: FOCUS-Japan surplus falls but sharp rises ahead.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Japan surplus falls but sharp rises ahead.

text.p: Japan's current account surplus shrank a sizeable 17 percent in March from a year earlier, but the drop in the politically sensitive number is expected to be the last for a while.

The Finance Ministry said on Wednesday that the March fall to 1.03 trillion yen ($8.7 billion) brought the surplus in the current account -- the broadest measure of trade in goods and services -- for the fiscal year ending in March to 7.18 trillion yen ($60.8 billion).
It was a drop of 24 percent from the previous year and the fourth year in a row that the surplus has fallen.

But economists dismissed the fall in March as due to special factors arising from a sales tax increase and warned the surplus would rise sharply in April, May and June, causing more trade tension with the United States.
U.S. officials have repeatedly warned they will not tolerate large increases in the surplus and that Tokyo should not return to relying on exports to fuel growth.

Economists said imports jumped in March as Japanese firms sought to feed a consumer spending rush ahead of the increase in the sales tax to five percent from three percent on April 1, pushing the trade surplus lower.
The surplus in trade alone fell 20.4 percent from a year earlier to 1.05 trillion yen ($8.8 billion).
However, empty pockets after the tax rise are likely to change the picture for the surplus, economists said.
"From April, the rise in the sales tax will mean domestic demand will fall and exports will jump as manufacturers shift their attention overseas," said Susumu Kato, chief economist at BZW Securities.
Import growth is also expected to take a beating as domestic demand weakens and crude oil imports fall after peak winter demand.
Rises in the April-June quarter would also look dramatic as they would be compared to large falls during the same period last year, economists said.

"For trading partners these are rises in the surplus in the midst of a weaker yen so (trade) problems will emerge," said BZW's Kato, who expects the surplus to nearly triple in April and help put upward pressure on the yen.
A stronger yen against the dollar makes imports into Japan cheaper, while exports from Japan become less competitive.

Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, however, has sought to play down the tension, saying that Japan's economic recovery was being led by domestic demand and urging leading nations to take a longer-term perspective on the issue.
The Finance Ministry also said on Wednesday that the current account surplus was unlikely to grow drastically in the mid-term.
But economists also noted the Finance Ministry had changed its strategy, referring not to the trade surplus but saying that it expected the surplus in goods and services to keep declining.
Many said, however, while they expect the United States to make a lot of noise on trade, they do not expect hysterics.

"At the moment, it's only car exports which are doing exceptionally well. It's not like before when all sorts of Japanese products were invading the world," said Junji Ota at Okasan Economic Research Institute. ($1=118 yen)
